How rods regenerate visual pigment
This illustrates the classical rod and retinal pigment epithelium cycle, not a timer for visual adaptation.
Rod outer segments face the pigment epithelium
Rod outer segments contain light-sensitive discs. Their tips face the retinal pigment epithelium, where retinoids can be exchanged.
Light changes the shape of retinal
After rhodopsin absorbs a photon, its 11-cis retinal changes into all-trans retinal, starting a visual signal.
All-trans retinol leaves the outer segment
All-trans retinal is released from rhodopsin and reduced to all-trans retinol, then transferred toward the pigment epithelium.
The pigment epithelium regenerates 11-cis retinal
In the pigment epithelium, all-trans retinol is first esterified. A reaction involving RPE65 leads to regeneration of 11-cis retinal.
Retinal returns to rebuild rhodopsin
11-cis retinal returns to the rod outer segment and binds opsin, regenerating rhodopsin for another photon.

How AII amacrine cells relay dim-light signals
This is one high-sensitivity rod pathway. Diagram brightness does not represent measured thresholds.
Rods detect faint light
In dim conditions, rods respond to very faint light and change their output to the next cell layer.
Rod bipolar cells pool the input
Multiple rods send information to a rod bipolar cell, which carries the pooled signal into the inner retina.
AII receives rod pathway signals
Rod bipolar terminals signal to the AII amacrine cell, which distributes the input through two different connections.
ON and OFF use different connections
AII passes signals to ON cone bipolar cells through gap junctions and inhibits the OFF pathway through glycinergic connections.
Ganglion cells report changes in light
ON and OFF circuits carry responses to increases and decreases in light toward ganglion cells. Other dim-light pathways are not shown.

How the corneal surface renews itself
This illustrates normal epithelial renewal, not injury, healing time, or treatment outcomes.
See the epithelium beneath the tear film
The tear film coats the outside of the cornea. Layers of epithelial cells beneath it form a transparent protective surface.
Renewal starts near the limbus
The limbus lies at the cornea-sclera boundary. Epithelial stem cells there supply daughter cells that can divide further.
New cells move inward from the edge
Daughter cells move inward along the basal layer. Colored tracks indicate renewal in different regions, not actual pigment.
Cells stratify and flatten toward the surface
Basal cells differentiate and move toward outer layers, eventually becoming flattened surface cells.
Replacement cells maintain the surface
Cells shed from the outer surface while cells from below replace them, keeping the epithelium continuous.
